title: Forged or doubted apostolic writings do not level Scripture with oral tradition
source_text: XXXIX. At, inquiunt, adversarii, Apostolis etiam multa scripta olim falso supposita sunt, & de quibusdam veris Apostolorum scriptis apud fideles ipsos dubitatum est. Igitur, si hoc argumentum traditionis non scriptae authoritatem tollit, ipsi Scripturae sua non constabit authoritas. Verum haec instantia nec apud nos Scripturae authoritatem evertit, nec argumenti nostri vim contra Pontificias traditiones imminuere potest. Neque enim Scripturae sacrae authoritatem quoad nos pendere volumus a testimonio doctorum Ecclesiae, sed Scripturam a fidelibus immediate & propter se suscipi statuimus, ut quae in se habeat divinitatis suae argumenta & notas insitas: adeoque quorumdam olim dubitatio de quibusdam Scripturae libris authoritati ejus apud nos nihil praejudicare potest. Nec etiam simpliciter traditiones rejicimus, quod quidam olim de iis dubitarunt, sed quia sunt Scripturae adversae, nec in se quicquam habent quo divina ipsis authoritas conciliari possit. Pontificii vero verbi Dei tam scripti, quam non scripti authoritatem quoad nos pendere statuunt a testimonio doctorum Ecclesiae. Adeoque, si prisci Ecclesiae Doctores, ex quorum relatione atque testimonio Ecclesia posteriorum saeculorum accepit traditiones suas, nec aliunde didicit illas ab Apostolis originem habere, si, inquam, prisci illi Ecclesiae Doctores de istis traditionibus tam incerti & varii erant, & eorum plerique in iis discernendis lapsi & decepti sunt, juxta placita Pontificiorum nulla certa authoritas ipsis constare potest.
pass_a_gloss: But, say the adversaries, many writings were also formerly falsely ascribed to the Apostles, and concerning certain true writings of the Apostles doubt was raised even among the faithful themselves. Therefore, if this argument takes away the authority of unwritten tradition, Scripture itself will not keep its authority. But this objection neither overturns Scripture's authority among us, nor can it weaken the force of our argument against Pontifical traditions. For we do not will that the authority of sacred Scripture as to us hang on the testimony of the Church's doctors, but we hold that Scripture is received by the faithful immediately and for its own sake, as that which has in itself the arguments and implanted marks of its divinity: and so former doubt of some people about certain books of Scripture cannot prejudice its authority among us. Nor do we reject traditions simply because some once doubted about them, but because they are adverse to Scripture, and have nothing in themselves by which divine authority can be won for them. But the Pontiffs hold that the authority of God's word, both written and unwritten, as to us hangs on the testimony of the Church's doctors. And so, if the early doctors of the Church — from whose report and testimony the Church of later ages received its traditions, and learned from nowhere else that they have origin from the Apostles — if, I say, those early doctors were so uncertain and various about those traditions, and most of them slipped and were deceived in discerning them, then according to the Pontiffs' own principles no certain authority can stand for them.
pass_b_english: Rome objects: forged 'apostolic' writings once circulated, and even true apostolic books were doubted among the faithful — so if that undercuts unwritten tradition, Scripture's authority falls too.

The objection fails on our side. We do not hang Scripture's authority on Church doctors' testimony. The faithful receive Scripture immediately, for its own sake, because it carries the marks of its divinity in itself.
Old doubts about certain books therefore do not prejudice Scripture among us.
We reject Rome's traditions not merely because some doubted them, but because they fight Scripture and have nothing in them that can claim divine authority.

Rome, by contrast, makes both written and unwritten 'word of God' hang on doctors' testimony. If those early doctors — the only chain by which later ages learned 'apostolic' traditions — were themselves uncertain, various, and often deceived, then on Rome's own principles those traditions have no certain authority.
